name: Raw egg consumption

lead: Some gym and looksmaxxing users drink or blend raw eggs for convenience, protein and choline, following the old strongman and Rocky Balboa image. Forum posts range from people reporting they drink a dozen or more at a time to threads arguing raw eggs are a meme.
Health authorities advise against eating raw eggs for vulnerable groups, and Wikipedia reports that egg protein is much less bioavailable raw than cooked.

paras: Raw egg contributes protein, fat and choline. Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin tightly, and cooking reduces this effect. Heat also kills Salmonella and makes the protein easier to digest.

Salmonella contamination of eggs is a recognised public health concern. Case-control research found raw eggs a leading risk factor for Salmonella Enteritidis infection, and raw egg allergy reactions have been reported even after tolerating cooked egg. Pasteurised eggs are sold as a lower-risk option.

lead: Raw egg consumption means eating or drinking uncooked eggs, commonly blended into shakes. The practice is associated with strength-sports culture, including the image of Rocky Balboa drinking raw eggs, and appears on looksmax.org as a cheap protein and choline source.[1][2]

Health sources describe two main concerns. Salmonella can contaminate eggs, either inside the egg from the hen or on a cracked shell, and heat destroys it.[3] Raw egg white also contains avidin, which binds biotin, and Wikipedia reports that egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable raw compared with roughly 91 percent cooked.[3][4]
Forum users disagree about whether raw eggs are worth it, with some posting large daily intakes and others arguing cooked eggs deliver more protein and nutrients.[2][5]
infobox: Avidin binding biotin in raw egg white

paras: Eggs can be eaten raw, for example in shakes, but health experts advise against it, especially for older adults, sick people and pregnant women, who are more vulnerable to salmonellosis.[3] A 2015 review notes that growing consumer interest in raw and unprocessed foods may be raising the risk of salmonellosis.[6]

Salmonella can reach the egg interior from the hen during laying or contaminate the shell, and it is killed instantly at about 71 degrees Celsius or at about 54.5 degrees Celsius if held long enough.[3] Eggs can be pasteurised in the shell at roughly 57 degrees Celsius for about 75 minutes, which reduces the risk.[3]

A 1988 JAMA paper described a more than sixfold rise in reported Salmonella Enteritidis infections in the northeastern United States between 1976 and 1986, and found that most outbreaks with an identified food source were linked to Grade A shell eggs or foods containing them.[7] A Dutch case-control study identified raw eggs as a predominant risk factor for Enteritidis infection.[8]

Health advice cited by Wikipedia includes refrigerating washed eggs, cooking them thoroughly, and not eating raw eggs; in the UK, hens are vaccinated against Salmonella and eggs are considered safe for 21 days.[3]

Wikipedia reports that cooking makes egg protein considerably easier to absorb, with roughly 51 percent bioavailability for raw egg protein against about 91 percent for cooked.[3] One forum poster argues that raw eggs provide marginally more choline (150 mg against 120 mg per egg, in the poster's figures) but less protein and fewer bioavailable nutrients overall, and another points out each raw egg has about 5.7 grams of protein.[2]

Avidin, found in the egg white of birds, reptiles and amphibians, binds biotin very tightly. Chicks fed raw egg white became biotin deficient despite biotin in the diet, and cooking above about 70 degrees Celsius largely removes its binding ability.[4]
A published report described anaphylactic reactions to raw egg in people who had passed challenges with cooked egg.[9]

No studies found of raw egg consumption for strength, muscle or appearance outcomes. Published research is limited to food-safety and epidemiology work on Salmonella from eggs,[6][7][8] allergy reports,[9] and nutrition data on protein and avidin summarised on reference pages.[3][4]

Looksmax.org has numerous threads in which users describe drinking a dozen or more raw eggs at a time, ask how to tolerate the taste, discuss fermenting eggs, or cite claims about choline benefits.[5] One thread titled as a question asks whether to switch from cooked to raw after months of eating six pasture-raised eggs a day, citing parasite concerns.[1] A thread titled 'Raw Eggs are a Meme' argues that raw eggs offer less protein and fewer bioavailable nutrients, and some replies say blending raw eggs into shakes is more convenient than cooking.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org raw eggs are posted as a protein-and-choline habit and are also criticised as inefficient.[2][5]

claims.claim: Raw eggs are a convenient, nutrient-rich protein source.
Raw eggs have more choline than cooked eggs.
Parasites and bacteria are not a concern.
Raw egg whites cause biotin deficiency.
